# Review of Inference


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What's Inference Again?

**Statistical Inference:** Estimating or testing claims about a **parameter** in a **population**, using a **statistic** in a **sample**.


- **Ex:** To understand proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians, we survey 40 students. 16 of the 40 are vegetarians.
  - **Population:** All Reedies
  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of all Reedies who are vegetarians
  - **Sample:** $n=40$ Reedies we surveyed
  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$
  

- We have seen [two types]{.underline} of inference procedures:

  1) **Confidence Intervals**
  
  2) **Hypothesis Testing**
  
- Let's review each...

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals {.smaller}

::: nonincremental
**Confidence Intervals:** plausible ranges of values for a parameter

**Ex:** What proportion of Reedies are vegetarians?

  - **Population:** All Reedies
  
  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians

  - **Sample:** $n=40$ students, of which 16 were vegetarian.

  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$
:::

::: fragment

Until now, we have learned to construct confidence intervals using **Bootstrap Distributions**:

:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width=50% .fragment}
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=3}
bs <- data.frame(outcome=c(
  rep("Yes",16),rep("No",24))) %>%
  rep_sample_n(size=40,replace=TRUE,reps=10000) %>%
  group_by(replicate) %>% summarize(phat=mean(outcome=="Yes"))
ggplot(bs, aes(x=phat))+geom_histogram(binwidth=0.025)+theme_minimal(base_size=15)+
  labs(x=expression("Bootstrap Sample Statistics,"~hat(p)))
```

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

  + **Bootstrap distribution:** Approximation of sampling distribution
    
  + Sample $n$ observations [with replacement]{.underline} from the [sample]{.underline}
    
  + For each "bootstrap sample", calculate/plot the statistic

:::

:::::


- **90% confidence interval:** Middle 90% is $(0.275, \ 0.525)$


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing {.smaller}

::: nonincremental
**Hypothesis Tests:** formal procedure for testing claims about a parameter

**Ex:** Are *less than* 50% of Reedies vegetarians?

  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians

  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$

  - **State Hypotheses:** $H_0: p=0.5$; $H_a: p<0.5$
  
:::

::: fragment
We need to construct the **Null Distribution:**
:::

::: fragment
::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

```{r eval=TRUE,echo=FALSE,fig.height=3.5,cache=TRUE}
sampling <- data.frame(
  outcome=c(rep("Yes",.5*10^6),rep("No",.5*10^6))) %>%
  rep_sample_n(size=40,replace=FALSE,reps=10000) %>%
  group_by(replicate) %>% 
  summarize(phat=mean(outcome=="Yes"))
ggplot(sampling, aes(x=phat))+
  geom_histogram(binwidth=0.025)+theme_minimal(base_size=15)+
  labs(x=expression("Sample Statistics"~hat(p)~" assuming"~H[0]))
```

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

  + **Null distribution:** Sampling distribution [assuming $H_0$]{.underline}
    
  + Many times, sample $n$ observations from [population assumed under $H_0$]{.underline}
    
  + For each "sample", calculate/plot the statistic
  
:::

:::::
:::


- **P-Value:** Area under curve to the left of $\widehat{p}$ is $0.07$

- **Compare to Significance Level:** Using $\alpha = 0.05$, we would *fail to reject* $H_0$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What's Similar?

- **Both inference procedures require a [sampling distribution of a statistic:]{.underline}**

  + [Confidence Intervals:]{.underline} Approximate with our bootstrap distribution (based on our sample)
  
  + [Hypothesis Testing:]{.underline} Simulate a sampling distribution assuming a population under $H_0$
  

<br>

- We've had to use simulation in `R` to find these "distributions of statistics"

  + In small samples, the code works and runs relatively quickly.
  
  + In larger samples, or with complicated statistics, this can be more computationally costly.


<br>

- **Could we do this work more efficiently? What did people use before computers?**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Theory-Based Inference

- Could we do this work more efficiently? **Yes! Use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT)!**

- Last lecture, we found:
  + Many sample statistics can be written as a **"sample mean"**
  + Sample means follow **Normal distributions**, with **formulas** for the mean and SD
  + We can **use the CLT** to characterize the distribution of a statistic!
  
::: fragment
::::: columns
::: {.column width=50%}

Instead of...
```{r echo=FALSE,out.width="100%",fig.asp=0.5}
bs <- data.frame(outcome=c(
  rep("Yes",16),rep("No",40-16))) %>%
  rep_sample_n(size=40,replace=TRUE,reps=10000) %>%
  group_by(replicate) %>% 
  summarize(phat=mean(outcome=="Yes"))
ggplot(bs, aes(x=phat))+theme_bw(base_size=15)+
  geom_histogram(binwidth=0.025,col="white")+
  labs(title="Sampling Distribution (based on computation)")
```

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

... we will instead use:
```{r out.width="100%",fig.asp=0.5}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.1,0.7,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.1,0.7,length=10000),mean=0.4,sd=sqrt(.4*.6/40)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+
  labs(title="Sampling Distribution (based on CLT)")
```

:::

:::::
:::


  
# Inference for a Single Proportion

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Central Limit Theorem
Suppose a simple random sample of size $n$ is drawn from a population with finite mean $\mu$ and finite standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $\bar{x}$ be the sample mean. When $n$ is large, then approximately
$$\bar{x} \sim Normal\Big(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\Big)$$
:::


<br>

**Goal:** Can we write a sample *proportion* $\widehat{p}$ as a sample *mean*?


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sample Proportion as a Sample Mean

- [Reminder]{.underline}: Let **$X\sim \text{Binomial}(n,p)$** distribution
    - $X$ is number of "successes" in **$n$ independent trials**, each trial has **probability of success, $p$**
    - $E(X) = np$ and $SD(X) = \sqrt{np(1-p)}$
  

- **Ex:** Polling (a SRS of) $n$ Reedies about vegetarianism

<br>

::::: columns
::: {.column width=50%}

::: {.nonincremental .fragment}
- **Key Trick 1:** Define
    - $X_1 = 1$ if Person 1 is vegetarian, 0 if not
    \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ $\vdots$
    - $X_n = 1$ if Person n is vegetarian, 0 if not
    
:::
    
- Note each $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

- **Key Trick 2:** The sample proportion, $\widehat{p}$ is a sample mean of these $X_i$'s!
$$
\begin{align}
\widehat{p} &= \frac{\text{Number of vegetarians}}{n} \\
&= \frac{X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_n}{n} \\
& = \bar{x}
\end{align}
$$

:::

:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Proportions and the CLT

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Central Limit Theorem
Suppose a simple random sample of size $n$ is drawn from a population with finite mean $\mu$ and finite standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $\bar{x}$ be the sample mean. When $n$ is large, then approximately
$$\bar{x} \sim Normal\Big(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\Big)$$
:::

::: fragment

[Bernoulli Random Variables:]{.underline} If $X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$, then
$$\mu = E(X_i) = p \ \ \ \text{and} \ \ \ \sigma = SD(X) = \sqrt{p(1-p)}$$

:::

- $\widehat{p} = \bar{x}$ 


- Plugging this in to CLT, **$\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}\Big(p, \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\Big)$**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Theory-Based Sampling Distribution for One Sample Proportion

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Theory-Based Sampling Distribution for One Sample Proportion 
Given a SRS of size $n$ drawn from a population with true proportion $p$, [when $n$ is large]{.underline} the sample proportion $\widehat{p}$ is distributed as:
$$\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}\Big(\ p, \ \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\ \Big)$$
:::


- Traditionally, $n$ is considered "large enough" when there are:

  - 10 or more "successes", [and]{.underline}
  
  - 10 or more "failures"


- Mathematically,

  - $n \widehat{p} \geq 10$, [and]{.underline}
  
  - $n (1 - \widehat{p}) \geq 10$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Word of Caution: CLT requires "large" $n$

::: fragment
$$\textbf{Theory-Based Sampling Distribution:} \ \ \  \widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}\Big(\ p, \ \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\ \Big)$$
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width=60% .fragment}
```{r fig.height=4, out.width="95%"}
set.seed(110)
p <- c(.5, .5, .01, .01)
n <- c(10, 100, 100, 1000)
b<-10000
sim_data <- data.frame(x = c(), example = c() )
for (i in 1:4){
  x <- rbinom(b, n[i], p[i])/n[i]
  sim_data <- rbind(sim_data, data.frame(x, example = rep(i, b)))
}
sim_summary <- sim_data %>% group_by(example) %>% 
  summarize(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))

g<-list()
for (i in 1:4){
  mu <- sim_summary[i,2] %>% pull()
  s <- sim_summary[i,3] %>% pull()
  g[[i]]<-sim_data %>% filter(example == i) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = x))+geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), binwidth =1/n[i], color = "white",fill ="steelblue")+
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mu, sd = s), color = "red", size = 1)+
    labs(x = expression(hat(p)), title = paste0("p=", p[i], ", n=", n[i]))
}

grid.arrange(g[[1]], g[[2]], g[[3]], g[[4]], ncol = 2)
```

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

- **"Large Enough $n$"**: 10 or more "successes" *and* "failures"

<br>

- **Q:** When does the (red) theory-based curve best/worst match the true sampling distribution? Why?

:::

:::::


# Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals (again) 

::: nonincremental
**Ex:** What proportion of Reedies are vegetarians?

  - **Population:** All Reedies
  
  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians

  - **Sample:** $n=40$ students, of which 16 were vegetarian.

  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$

:::

::: fragment
**Sampling Distribution:**
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width=2%}

:::

::: {.column width=55%}

  + *Theoretical* sampling distribution: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(p,\sqrt{p(1-p)/n})$



  + For *our best guess*, **substitute $\widehat{p}=0.4$ for $p$**: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(0.4,\sqrt{0.4(1-0.4)/40})$

:::

::: {.column width=43% .fragment}
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=4}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.1,0.7,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.1,0.7,length=10000),mean=0.4,sd=sqrt(.4*.6/40)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)))+
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Sampling Distribution")
```

:::

:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------
  
## Confidence Intervals (again) 

::: nonincremental
**Ex:** What proportion of Reedies are vegetarians?

  - **Population:** All Reedies
  
  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians

  - **Sample:** $n=40$ students, of which 16 were vegetarian.

  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$

:::


**Sampling Distribution:**

::::: columns
::: {.column width=2%}

:::

::: {.column width=55% .nonincremental}

  + *Theoretical* sampling distribution: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(p,\sqrt{p(1-p)/n})$


  + For *our best guess*, **substitute $\widehat{p}=0.4$ for $p$**: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(0.4,\sqrt{0.4(1-0.4)/40})$
  
  + **Quantiles** of this distribution give us confidence intervals, ex. $(0.273, \ 0.527)$

:::

::: {.column width=43%}
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=4}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.1,0.7,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.1,0.7,length=10000),mean=0.4,sd=sqrt(.4*.6/40)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)))+
  stat_function(fun = function(x){dnorm(x,.4,sqrt(.4*.6/40))},
                xlim = c(0.273,  0.527), geom = "area", fill = "steelblue") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "Middle 90%", x = .4, y = 2.5,color="white",size=5) +
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Sampling Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(.273,.4,.527))
```

:::

:::::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals: Process Check 

When making (percentile) confidence intervals using **computational** methods, we:

1) Specify our population, and parameter

2) Collect a sample, and calculate the statistic

3) Create a bootstrap distribution to approximate the sampling distribution

4) Use quantiles of the approximated sampling distribution to make a confidence interval

<br>


::: fragment
**Q:** Which steps above are the **same** and which are **different** with our new "theory-based" way?
:::

- **Only #3 is different!**

- "Old Way": Collect bootstrap samples 

- "Theory-based Way": Use CLT, which gives a "theoretical" sampling distribution of
$$\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(\widehat{p},\sqrt{\widehat{p}(1-\widehat{p})/n})$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(1.5)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing (again) 

::: {.nonincremental}
**Ex:** Are *less than* 50% of Reedies vegetarians?

  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians

  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$

  - **State Hypotheses:** $H_0: p=0.5$; $H_a: p<0.5$

:::

::: fragment
**Null Distribution:**
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width=2%}

:::

::: {.column width=57%}

  + *Theoretical* sampling distribution: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(p,\sqrt{p(1-p)/n})$


  + For *null distribution*, **substitute "null value" $p=0.5$**: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(0.5,\sqrt{0.5(1-0.5)/40})$

:::

::: {.column width=41% .fragment}
```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=5}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.2,0.8,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.2,0.8,length=10000),mean=0.5,sd=sqrt(.5*.5/40)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)))+
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Null Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(.3,.7,by=0.1))
```

:::

:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing (again) 

::: {.nonincremental}
**Ex:** Are *less than* 50% of Reedies vegetarians?

  - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians

  - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p} = 16/40 = 0.4$

  - **State Hypotheses:** $H_0: p=0.5$; $H_a: p<0.5$

**Null Distribution:**
:::


::::: columns
::: {.column width=2%}

:::

::: {.column width=57%}

::: nonincremental
  + *Theoretical* sampling distribution: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(p,\sqrt{p(1-p)/n})$

  + For *null distribution*, **substitute "null value" $p=0.5$**: $\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}(0.5,\sqrt{0.5(1-0.5)/40})$
  
  + **P-Value:** In this case, area under curve to the left of $\widehat{p}=0.4$. Here, $\text{P-Value}=0.07$.

:::

  + Compare the P-Value to your significance level ($\alpha$).

:::

::: {.column width=41%}

```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=5}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.2,0.8,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.2,0.8,length=10000),mean=0.5,sd=sqrt(.5*.5/40)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)))+
  stat_function(fun = function(x){dnorm(x,.5,sqrt(.5*.5/40))},
                xlim = c(.2,  0.4), geom = "area", fill = "steelblue") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "p-value=\n0.07", x = .3, y = 2,color="black",size=7) +
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Null Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(.3,.7,by=0.1))
```

:::

:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Tests: Process Check {.smaller}

When conducting hypothesis tests, we:

1) Specify our population, and parameter

2) State null ($H_0$) and alternative ($H_a$) hypotheses, e.g.,
$$
H_0: p = p_0 \qquad \qquad H_a: p \neq p_0 \ \ \text{or} \ \ p < p_0 \ \ \text{or} \ \ p > p_0
$$

3) Collect a sample, and calculate the statistic

4) Create a null distribution

5) Use "areas/proportions" of the null distribution distribution to calculate the p-value

6) Compare p-value to our rejection threshold $\alpha$, and make a conclusion

<br>

- **Q:** Which steps in the above are the **same** in both the "old" way of doing hypothesis tests, and this new "theory-based" way? Which steps are **different**?

- **Only #4 is different!** (again, the distribution we use comes from theory instead of simulation)

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(1.5)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Recap: Theory-Based Inference

$$\textbf{CLT-Based Sampling Distribution:} \ \ \  \widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}\Big(\ p, \ \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\ \Big)$$

- The general steps we take are the [same]{.underline} as before, but we **now use the CLT instead of simulation to find sampling distributions**.

::::: columns
::: {.column width=45% .fragment}

$$\textbf{Confidence Intervals}$$
$$\text{Sampling Distribution of } p$$
$$(\text{Plug in statistic, }\color{red}{\widehat{p}})$$

$$\text{Normal}\Bigg(\color{red}{\widehat{p}}, \ \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}})}{n}} \ \Bigg)$$

:::

::: {.column width=10%}

:::

::: {.column width=45% .fragment}

$$\textbf{Hypothesis Testing}$$
$$\text{Null Distribution}$$
$$(\text{Plug in null value, }\color{red}{p_0})$$

$$\text{Normal}\Bigg(\color{red}{p_0}, \ \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{p_0}(1-\color{red}{p_0})}{n}} \ \Bigg)$$

:::

:::::
